note_claims.claim: The presenting complaint is fever and right earache.
Fever has been present since Monday evening (3 days), with a maximum temperature of 38.9 °C at home.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear and was unsettled overnight.
The patient has been eating less but drinking well and passing urine normally.
The patient vomited once on Tuesday and has had no vomiting since.
The patient has had a runny nose for about a week preceding the current symptoms.
The patient has no rash.
The patient has not had chickenpox, although her brother had it two weeks ago.
The patient is alert and playing this morning.
The patient's immunisations are up to date.
The patient takes no regular medications and has no known drug allergies.
The patient weighs 14 kilograms.
The patient's vital signs are Temperature 38.4 °C, Heart Rate 130, and Breathing Rate 26.
The patient has warm peripheries and a capillary refill time under two seconds.
The left tympanic membrane is normal.
The right tympanic membrane is red and bulging.
The patient's throat is mildly erythematous.
The chest examination is clear.
The impression is Right acute otitis media.
There are no features of serious bacterial illness.
There is a recent chickenpox contact.
The plan includes regular analgesia: paracetamol 180 mg (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL) up to four times daily and ibuprofen 100 mg (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times daily with food.
A back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily for 5 days is provided, to be collected only if the patient does not improve after three days or if she worsens.
A leaflet on chickenpox is given.
Urgent help (999 or A&E) is required if the patient develops a non-blanching rash, becomes very drowsy or hard to rouse, has breathing difficulty, or stops drinking and not passing urine.
Contact the GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if there is ear discharge, or if the patient is not improving after three days.
The patient should report if she develops chickenpox and seems very unwell.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician asks the patient what has been happening.
The patient has had a temperature and keeps pulling at her ear.
The relative corrects the timing of the fever: it was Monday evening (3 days), not Tuesday night.
The temperature measured last night on the ear thermometer was 38.9.
The patient is pulling at the right ear, mostly.
The patient states, 'My ear hurts.'
The patient is not eating much but is drinking okay (juice and milk).
The patient is in pants during the day but is still weeing normally, a few times today already.
The patient was sick once on Tuesday, but not since.
The patient had a runny nose for about a week before all this started.
The patient has no rash, and her brother had chickenpox two weeks ago.
The patient has never had chickenpox.
The patient is grumpy but herself and was playing with her brother this morning.
The patient reports no problems breathing.
The patient is healthy and all her vaccinations are done.
The patient takes no regular medicines and has no allergies.
The patient gives Calpol only when she seems really bad.

The patient's weight is 14 kilograms. Her temperature is 38.4 °C, heart rate is 130, and breathing rate is 26. Her hands and feet are warm and the capillary refill is under two seconds. She is alert and chatting.
The patient states, 'Rabbit's ears are fine.'
The clinician examines the ears and notes the left eardrum is normal, while the right eardrum is red and bulging. The patient's throat is a little red.

The clinician suggests it looks like a middle ear infection on the right side, which usually gets better on its own within three days or so, even without antibiotics, and antibiotics don't make much difference to the pain.
The clinician suggests giving paracetamol 180 milligrams (7.5 mL of 120 mg/5 mL) up to four times a day and ibuprofen 100 milligrams (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times a day with food for pain.
The clinician offers a back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 milligrams three times a day for 5 days, to be collected only if she is not improving after three days or if she is getting worse.

The clinician advises calling 999 or going straight to A&E if the patient gets a rash that doesn't fade when pressed with a glass, becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, is struggling to breathe, or stops drinking and isn't weeing.
The clinician advises contacting the GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if there is any discharge from the ear, or if the patient is not improving after three days.
The clinician advises that the patient may get chickenpox in the next week or so since she has been exposed, and to let them know if she seems very unwell with it.
